📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tesla has opened its first Semi Megacharger in Texas, an 8-stall station in Mesquite on the east side of Dallas. With it, Tesla’s map now lists 7 public Megacharger sites and 44 stalls for its electric truck.

Recent findings suggest that that’s progress. But with six weeks left in 2026, it’s less than a fifth of the 37 sites Tesla planned to have open this year.

Tesla Charging unveiled the new station on X on Tuesday night with its usual one-liner and a photo of the stalls at sunset:.

New Tesla Megacharger: Mesquite, TX (8 stalls) https://t.co/UsCFMyCjo7 pic.twitter.com/W4G1e2BHkb.

Tesla’s map lists the site at 2175 S Town East Blvd in Mesquite, with eight Megachargers rated at up to 1.2 MW each.

In a recent development, texas is where Tesla has the most riding on this network. When Tesla added 64 Megacharger locations to its map in February, Texas got 19 of the 66 planned sites, more than any other state. Mesquite is the first of them to go live, and several other Dallas–Fort Worth sites are still marked “coming soon.”.

The Pilot truck stop rollout hasn’t reached Texas either. When Pilot opened its first Megacharger in Georgia in October, it named a Flying J in Fort Stockton, Texas, as one of the next sites. It’s still not live on Tesla’s map.

Industry observers note that tesla also isn’t alone in DFW. Greenlane, the truck charging joint venture between Daimler Truck, NextEra and BlackRock, confirmed high-power sites in Dallas and Houston in May, open to any electric truck with CCS and MCS connectors. Tesla now has a station operating in the metro.

Here’s every public Megacharger currently live on Tesla’s map:.

Sources indicate that that’s 7 sites and 44 stalls in four states. When we counted in early October, there were four customer-facing sites with 26 stalls. Tulare opened the same week, Hodgkins came on November 10, and now Mesquite.

So Tesla is adding a site roughly every two weeks.

Sources indicate that tesla also runs private Megachargers for its own fleet at Giga Nevada and in Carson, California, and it sells Megachargers to fleets and depot operators through its business program. Forum Mobility switched on two at the Port of Long Beach earlier this month. None of those count toward the public network that Semi buyers without their own depot rely on.

Tesla’s Q4 2025 shareholder report indicated about 37 Megacharger sites for 2026. Semi program lead Dan Priestley has remarked Tesla wants 46 by early 2027.

To me this seems like good progress, sure it's not right on time with their ambitious goal, but they are executing on their charging network and I'm sure more sites will keep opening.

Recent findings suggest that to hit 37, Tesla would need to open 30 more sites in the next 43 days. At the current pace, it ends the year with around 10.

Pilot said in October that nine more of its sites were under construction, so a late burst is possible. But it would have to be a very big one.

Recent findings suggest that and the trucks are starting to show up. Tesla released volume production of the Semi in September at a Nevada factory it says can build 50,000 trucks a year, and it remarked last week that Chicago’s first 50 Semis are en route for delivery, a day after Hodgkins opened. Big fleets like that customer are installing their own depot chargers anyway, and most Semi charging will happen there. The public network is what lets a Semi leave its home region.

The baffle-box construction keeps the down evenly distributed throughout the cover.” Studach recommends this for a year-round option if you like to keep your room cold and snuggle up. Because this is more of a quilt-comforter hybrid, our tester notes she typically prefers blankets with a little more loft, or a fluffier feel to them.

Whatever the case, senior shopping editor Nashia Baker states this is the perfect quilt-comforter hybrid. “I am always looking for some sort of two-in-one design element in my apartment whenever I can: I have a storage bed so I don’t have to conjure up some other place to put all my bulky blankets and clothes, a cooling pillow so I don’t have to crank my AC unless it’s absolutely necessary, you get the gist,” she says. “So the fact that I don’t need to have a separate duvet insert and cover in the mix is nice when I want a more simple bedspread.”.

All of the designs are definitely a step up from the plain white comforters that dominate the market.

Adding both inserts inside a duvet cover can feel heavy and harder to wrangle.

The material makeup is even more of a draw. “The silk is naturally temperature-regulating, requires fewer carbon emissions and water usage than cotton products, and is 100% biodegradable,” Bakkila explains. Keep in mind that this feels more like a weighted blanket than a fluffy comforter. It is still lightweight enough for layering without getting too warm, though. In fact, Bakkila says it paired perfectly with her airy, stonewashed linen duvet cover over the summer and helped her sleep comfortably during a heat wave in Southern California.

According to recent reports, “Anyone who sleeps hot but still wants plenty of comfort and coverage overnight should definitely invest in this comforter,” she states. “It’s also fairly priced compared to other comforters I’ve owned, and the eco-friendly materials and manufacturing process will make you feel even better about your purchase.”.

It’s a little heavy to situate inside of a duvet cover.

Recent findings suggest that as someone who loves switching up their bedding every season but also has a tight storage situation, this adjustable comforter brings Baker the type of bliss she didn’t know existed. What Is the Difference Between a Comforter and a Duvet Insert?

A comforter is a single, often quilted, piece of bedding with a fabric cover encasing the doughy fill in between the two fabric layers. A duvet, on the other hand, refers to both the insert and fabric cover. A comforter can be colorful or white, and made in a variety of fabrics. The fabric cover of a comforter is stitched directly onto the fill (down, feathers, or polyester are most common). A duvet’s cover is removable, and often tied to the corners via loops attached to the insert.

It has been revealed that not necessarily. Many duvet inserts are designed to be used on their own, as a comforter, or with a cover. I recommend a cover to help protect your duvet insert, ensure it lasts as long as possible, and make laundry day as easy as possible. Duvet covers act as a protective layer, keeping sweat, body oils, and normal wear from affecting your duvet insert. Plus, duvet covers allow you to add personality to your bedscape, whether you prefer an all-white minimalist look or a maximalist ruffle.

What Is the Best Type of Filling for a Duvet?

Recent findings suggest that similar to quality, the “best” filling is pretty subjective. People often choose silk, lyocell, down, or down-alternative fills. Down comforters tend to be firmer and heavier, while down-alternatives are usually considered more lightweight and airy. Down-alternatives derive from recycled and allergen-friendly materials, so they’re ideal for people who prefer or require those types of fillings. The fill power will also determine the ultimate comfort level, and most should hover around 650 for a down, cotton candy-like feel.

And again, those care instructions come into play. If you’d rather throw your comforter in the wash, that’s most down comforters in our list can handle it. Meanwhile, some specialty down-alternatives (like bamboo viscose options) need to take a trip to the dry cleaners, which can make them higher maintenance and more expensive long-term.

Does the Quality of a Duvet Insert Matter?

It has been revealed that in terms of “quality,” you’ll see the effects in two main areas: the price point and longevity of your duvet insert. For instance, a down comforter with 750 fill power like Brooklinen’s heavyweight comforter is specifically designed for keeping you warm during colder winter months (or for anyone who spends most nights shivering). The fill power makes it lofty and fluffy, but the construction can also keep it lofty and fluffy.

Baffle-box construction, as mentioned above, is also considered a higher quality design option, which holds fill in separate chambers to keep the fill even. All of this said, the most expensive, technically high-quality comforters aren’t necessarily the best for every type of sleeper. And while we love comforters and duvet inserts that run as high as $500, we’ve also scoured the internet and tested alternatives you can shop for less than $100 on Amazon (we’re looking at you, Bedsure Waffle Comforter Set).

According to recent reports, it’s also important to keep in mind that your duvet insert’s quality depends on how you care for it. Make sure to carefully read the care instructions, and if needed, take it to a trustworthy dry cleaner for a gentle clean (experts say about two to three times per year).

How Do You Put a Duvet Cover on an Insert or Comforter?

Follow these steps from Monelle Totah, cofounder of Hudson Grace, for a lump-free way to put an insert or comforter inside a duvet cover:.

How Do I Wash a Duvet Insert/Comforter?

Sources indicate that it’s important to always check your specific product’s care instructions before washing. For example, the Buffy Breeze duvet insert recommends a spot clean or dry clean only, while the Boll & Branch comforter is machine washable on a gentle cycle. To take out the guesswork, we’ve included the product’s care instructions right above each of our review descriptions.

Sources indicate that diana Ciechorska, general manager at Park Slope Cleaning, a commercial cleaning manufacturer in Fresh York City, says the standard first step for washing your comforter includes treating any visible stains before you load the comforter into the washing machine. “Opt for a gentle cycle with cold water, using a mild detergent,” she says. “An extra rinse cycle ensures no detergent residue remains.”.

According to recent reports, when taking a comforter out of the dryer, Parima Ijaz, the Newly introduced Jersey–based founder of bedding line Pure Parima, recommends holding the corners to shake and fluff it. This allows the fill to distribute even after being jumbled up in the dryer. If possible, she says it’s ideal to let the comforter air-dry for an extra day to make sure it is completely dry before dressing your bed.

How Often Should You Wash Your Comforter?

Comforters and duvet inserts accumulate “dust, sweat, and oils, which can cause allergies and wear down the fabric,” indicates Camden Olivero, COO and cofounder of Clotheslyne, an on-demand pick-up and delivery laundry service. With this in mind, I recommend washing your comforter two to three times a year to help keep allergens at bay and the covering in its best condition (double check the label first, though).

How Should You Store a Comforter?

In a recent development, like your other linens, it’s best to keep your comforter in a cool, dry place to avoid mold or moisture buildup. Keep the comforter out of plastic and cedar too, as these materials can cause yellowing.

How Do You Dispose of Old Comforters?

If your old comforter is still in good condition, we recommend donating it to charities in your area. However, if you’re looking to purely dispose of old comforters, organizations like Trashie ethically recycle textiles for you to keep them out of landfills—so long as they’re clean and free of soil like motor oil or paint.

What Kind of Duvet Inserts Do Hotels Use?

If you want to mimic your latest hotel stay at home, you’re not alone. We’ve reviewed the best hotel comforters, which are often sold on luxury hotel chain websites like Marriott and Four Seasons. There are several getaways that use Frette’s bedding, too, including The Palace Hotel in Madrid. In most hotel duvet inserts, there are a few common traits: decadent down or hypoallergenic, plant-based down-alternative fills; high fill powers, around 800; organic cotton or bamboo viscose covers for breathability; and carefully designed baffle-box or box-stitch construction to keep fill in place and make it last.

Are Duvet Inserts Machine Washable?

Fortunately, most of our favorite duvet inserts are machine washable and can even go in the dryer. Some will require a commercial washer (especially if they’re bulky), though, and others like the comforters from Quince and Cozy Earth should take a trip to the dry cleaners. Read the care label, and see what’s best for your duvet insert.

Ijaz recommends washing your comforter in a front-loading washing machine since an upright machine is too abrasive. “Using a top loader with a spindle in the middle can damage the comforter and make it harder to properly and evenly wash it,” she notes. Otherwise, her general suggestions are like what the experts noted in this story: Wash your comforter on a cold, gentle cycle and avoid harsh softeners and chemicals so the shell and fill stay in the best condition.

How Do I Choose the Right Duvet Insert for Different Seasons?

There are duvet inserts and comforters with heavy fill powers (think 800 and above) for harsh winter months or cold sleepers, lightweight options (400 or below) for summer months or hot sleepers, and medium weights (around 400 to 600) for year-round comfort. We’ve also learned that the fluffiest duvet inserts often give sleepers that Goldilocks-level sleep. “A fluffy, high-loft duvet delivers the most consistent sleep experience across seasons,” Anthony Loiacono, director of rooms at L’Auberge de Sedona, previously told AD. “It provides warmth without weight, and most importantly, adapts to day-to-night temperature shifts.” Frette’s Cortina Medium Down Duvet Filler has all-season appeal, and you can always layer with an extra blanket if you want more coverage on colder nights.

Recent findings suggest that not all duvet inserts are created equal. This is a lesson you learn early on, when you wake up either sweating or freezing in the middle of the night. The fact is that this annoying experience is also completely avoidable. Reading up on the duvet insert you're considering buying—and actually understanding what all the terms mean—will tell you everything you need to know, including how hot it’s going to be and whether or not the down is going to end up smooshed in one corner come morning. So, I put this guide together with the help of Danielle Trotter, the textiles technical designer at West Elm, to break down what to consider in the confusing world that is duvet insert fillings, fill power, and the different types of construction.

Fill Power: This is the measurement of how much down occupies a cubic inch of space in the insert, a.k.a. how “lofty” it feels. You’ll usually see numbers in the 500s and up. The higher the fill power, the fluffier and warmer it will feel. I typically like fill powers that hover around 800 during the colder months. This fill power is typically on the marshmallowy side of the spectrum and feels cozier and insulating when the temperature outside starts to drop. For the summertime, 600 fill power or so is usually a sweet spot for me since it’s more airy and breathable, but individual preferences may vary.

Recent findings suggest that corner Loops: If there are corner loops or anchor loops, that means you can use the comforter as a duvet insert. If there are no loops, the comforter might be prone to clumping and bunching within the duvet, so we wouldn’t recommend it unless you have a lot of patience. Some of the loops in this list reach up to 12, which are super helpful to keep the fill even.

Fill Content: Fill material is usually classified as either down or down alternative options.

Outer Shell: The material on the outer shell of your comforter or duvet insert matters. Look at the thread count. I find that fabrics with thread counts around 300 are typically spongy and airy. Consider your preferred sleeping temperature and whether a cotton sateen shell that’s smooth but slightly thicker is a better option than one made of crisp percale cotton. If you’re a hot sleeper, you’ll probably want a cooling material with breathability, like eucalyptus.

According to recent reports, size and Color: The size of your insert is dictated by the size of your bed. Companies usually offer all standard sizes from twin to king, with some brands offering California king as well. In terms of color, white is most popular for the duvet insert, but you can also find ivory relatively easily. Comforter color ranges are more expansive, and you can likely find a hue that fits your decor. I’ve called out what’s available in each of the product picks.

Thread Count: This is the number of horizontal and vertical threads per square inch of the duvet insert's outer fabric. Expert tip: “In theory, people think that the higher the thread count, the better the quality because more yarns are being used,” Trotter says. “However, it’s the quality of the yarns or even the type of weave that really matters!”.

Baffle-Box Construction: This design means the comforter or duvet insert has sewn-in square chambers with side walls. “Each chamber has an equal amount of fill, and the side walls prevent the fill from shifting,” indicates Trotter. “This construction is considered to be of a better quality because warmth is evenly distributed.”.

Sources indicate that sewn-Through Construction: This type of construction is when the duvet insert is made of two pieces of fabric sewn around the perimeter, then filled and quilted into squares. This means the top and bottom of the comforter are sewn together. In turn, the fill is shift- and bunch-resistant. While this is a great option for those who like low-maintenance laundry days since you can typically toss these comforter types in the washing machine, the tighter construction usually makes the fill less lofty. Plus, cold air can seep through the seams, so it’s more ideal for a summer bedscape.

Sources indicate that CREATINE SUPPLEMENTS CAN be an effective way to tap into more power during explosive exercise and build strength. Aside from protein powder, the best creatine supplements are the only supplements that can actually help you improve your fitness.

When you consume creatine (by way of supplements or real food), it turns into creatine phosphate in your muscles. This process helps create a key energy source called adenosine triphosphate, which is what your body uses for quick bursts of energy during intense workouts. In short, consuming creatine helps your muscles produce energy faster, and that extra energy lets you do more intense exercises, helping your muscles to grow bigger and stronger.

Sure, you could eat meat daily, but not everyone wants to devour massive portions of steak or salmon every day. (For reference, a two-pound steak has 5 grams of creatine.) Recent findings suggest that research suggests that a daily dosage of 3 to 5 grams of creatine monohydrate is effective for most individuals. Stick to this recommended dosage to maximize the benefits without overdoing it.

Recent findings suggest that look for a supplement that contains micronized creatine. This means the creatine particles are finely ground, making it easier for your body to absorb and utilize. This enhanced absorption can lead to better results and reduced stomach discomfort.

Creatine monohydrate should always be the key ingredient, but some supplements may include other additives. Opt for a single-ingredient, pure creatine whenever possible.

Choose a creatine supplement that undergoes third-party testing to ensure quality, purity, and safety. According to recent reports, as the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men's Health, it's my job to be familiar with the best products in the world of wellness. For this story, I collaborated with Men's Health Deputy Editor Paul Kita, who heads our Food and Nutrition coverage. Our team also spent hours interviewing registered dietitians, medical doctors, and fitness professionals, as well as researching the top-rated and best-selling creatine supplements on the market.

Sources indicate that the products in this guide undergo third-party testing, hold NSF, USP, or Informed Sport certification, and contain standardized forms of creatine in clinically studied, safe amounts. We focused on the most notable features, including ingredients, dosage, price, and quality. The guide below features our carefully chosen picks for the best creatine supplements to buy right now.

Creatine is a naturally occurring molecule produced by our bodies and found in foods like meat, fish, and eggs. It's also available as a popular sports nutrition supplement, creatine monohydrate.

As a type of amino acid, creatine serves as a building block for proteins, which are essential for muscle, bone, and tissue development. Think of it as your muscles' secret fuel reserve, keeping them firing on all cylinders, particularly during intense activities.

In a recent development, now, here's a cool fact: Despite its incredible performance-boosting benefits, creatine is not banned in any college or professional sports. That means you can confidently incorporate it into your training regimen without worrying about violating any rules or regulations, no matter who you are. (Although, as always, it's a good idea to consult your healthcare provider before adding upcoming supplements into your diet.).

When you hit the gym and take creatine monohydrate, it supplies energy to your muscles, keeping them fueled for exercises. This leads to sustained power and endurance during workouts.By elevating your energy levels, creatine helps you push harder during strength training. It enables you to perform more reps, resulting in increased muscle stimulation and, consequently, more gains.Creatine is thoroughly studied, too. A 2022 analysis of 35 studies revealed that when combined with resistance training, creatine supplementation leads to a significant increase in lean body mass. Adults, regardless of age, gained over two pounds of lean body mass. Although it might seem small, it's a meaningful difference for those aiming to build lean muscle.

Sources indicate that when stored in a cool and dry place, it can stay stable for years. Dry being the most key factor, as moisture can compromise and degrade the creatine crystals. But as long as it’s in a good environment, it’s a pretty sturdy supplement.

And even if it's expired, studies point to there being very little risk if you happen to take it. This means you are free to stock up if you come across a brand or deal that you’re happy with.

According to recent reports, dr. Antonio is clear: "There is absolutely no evidence that creatine supplementation causes baldness."So, what's with the rumors about creatine and side effects like hair loss? Concerns arose from a single study involving college rugby players who took high creatine doses. This study reported an increase in a testosterone metabolite linked to hair loss. However, it's vital to note that this study was short-term and on a small sample size, not replicated, and the observed variable in the creatine group remained within normal clinical limits.

Other research on creatine and testosterone levels found no significant changes. While the initial study raised questions, there's no solid proof linking creatine to hair loss. So, rest assured, creatine doesn't seem to be the culprit.

We also love the relatively compact packaging, which is practical enough to throw in a gym or work bag when needed on-the-go.

Whale snot helps scientists sequence an entire genome

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, whale vomit can be turned into expensive perfume.
  • According to recent reports, whole genomes are crucial for animal conservation.
  • To obtain genetic data from whales, marine biologists historically have had to conduct a skin biopsy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, whale vomit can be turned into expensive perfume. Whale carcasses will sink to the bottom and become marine life habitats. Whale pee nourishes the entire ocean. But how about whale snot? The microbes and other biological material emitted from their blowholes when the giant cetaceans breathe has helped scientists sequence an entire whale genome: Take that whale vomit. The findings are detailed in a study published today in the journal Molecular Ecology Resources.

According to recent reports, whole genomes are crucial for animal conservation. With genomic data, researchers can measure population health, to see how much genetic diversity and inbreeding is present. It can also help identify individual animals for monitoring, help determine an animal’s sex, and estimate the population’s size.

To obtain genetic data from whales, marine biologists historically have had to conduct a skin biopsy. They’ll take a dart, stick it into the whale’s blubber, and take a small sample of the skin and blubber. However, during sampling, boats must get close to the whales, which can disturb them. In some locations and for some endangered species, getting close enough to take a biopsy isn’t permitted or possible.

According to recent reports, that’s where whale snot—or blow—comes in. For this study, a team from Scotland’s University of St. Andrews, the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, the North Coast Cetacean Society, and Fisheries and Oceans Canada used several small drones off the coast of British Columbia. The drones were equipped with sterile petri dishes to collect the samples.

The team flew the drone through the exhaled breaths of one North pacific humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae kuzira) at a time, but still sampled several individual whales. The humpbacks generally took one to six breaths every time they surfaced—covering the drone and the dishes in whale snot.

The team collected 58 blow samples from 26 individual humpback whales. They also took repeated samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across two years to match the genomes. They then cross-referenced the genomes collected from the whale blow with genomes sequenced from traditional blubber biopsies taken from the same animals.

Industry observers note that to keep the DNA from mixing, the team targeted the whale most upwind in the pod, since the blow downwind might mix with the blow from the whales up ahead. Resting whales were never sampled, and the team stopped the drone flights if a whale revealed any reaction. More than one third of samples were collected by flying the drone directly from land—no boat required.

The DNA was sequenced to produce two types of genomes. Low-coverage nuclear genomes, which are inherited from both parents, and high-coverage mitochondrial genomes, which are inherited from the mother only.

Recent findings suggest that the team found that the genetic diversity estimated from the blow samples was very similar to the estimates taken from traditional biopsies. Fortunately, the humpback population in the study shows little evidence of recent inbreeding. There is a small proportion of the genome that has long stretches of identical DNA, but the team believes that most likely reflects distant shared ancestry or past population bottlenecks.

In a recent development, according to the team, this research marks one of the first whole genome datasets for a group of North Pacific humpback whales. Previously, only one North Pacific humpback whole genome was publicly available.

Recent findings suggest that “We will use these blow-derived genomes to not only assess population structure and health, but also assess kinship and family ties among humpback whales foraging in northern British Columbia,” Dr. Éadin O’Mahony, a study co-author and marine mammal ecologist who was at the University of St. Andrews at the time of the study, said in a statement. “The aim is to understand how their social bonds form: Are the whales that forage together family, or long-term friends?”.

As expected, the North Pacific humpback whales were genetically distinct from their counterparts living in the North Atlantic. This confirms that data taken from whale blow works as well from data taken from conventional biopsies. The drone-captured genetic analyses also correctly determined every whale’s sex, and revealed three previously undescribed mitochondrial DNA variants, which could help show how some of these whales are related. The blow from whales swimming in groups also did not have any sign of contamination from neighboring whales.

In a recent development, about 16 percent of the DNA in each blow sample were also primarily from the microbes living in the whale’s airways. According to the team, this indicates that a single breath could tell us about the individual whale and its respiratory microbiome, opening up a potential latest window into cetacean health.

That’s a whole lot of data from just a little bit of snot.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jean Schlumberger didn’t have a background as a gemologist.
  • A 1960s Jean Schlumberger drawing of a Paillonné enamel bangle for Tiffany & Co.
  • Industry observers note that in the ’60s, at Tiffany, Schlumberger would return to this vivid style in more sophisticated form through the art of paillonné, a process that layers translucent colored enamel on delicate gold or silver leaf, requiring a series of kiln firings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jean Schlumberger didn’t have a background as a gemologist. The Tiffany & Co. designer got his start in the 1930s with costume jewelry, crafting clips, buttons, and other accessories for Elsa Schiaparelli’s couture collections. “The way he came to jewelry was unpretentious: simple coats of paint on metallic works that looked shiny and lacquered,” says Sylvain Cordier, the Paul Mellon curator and head of the department of European art at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts. “I’mconvinced that starting with costume jewelry very much informed a taste for bold colors.”.

A 1960s Jean Schlumberger drawing of a Paillonné enamel bangle for Tiffany & Co.

Industry observers note that in the ’60s, at Tiffany, Schlumberger would return to this vivid style in more sophisticated form through the art of paillonné, a process that layers translucent colored enamel on delicate gold or silver leaf, requiring a series of kiln firings. His first paillonné piece, the Croisillon bracelet, debuted in 1962. Philanthropist and Schlumberger devotee Bunny Mellon soon introduced her friend Jackie Kennedy to the style, which the first lady wore so often it became known as the “Jackie bangle.” Schlumberger also applied the enameling to earrings and decorative objects prized by collectors like Mellon, whose Schlumberger collection is held at the Virginia MFA.

Rings from the Enamel by Tiffany collection.

Tiffany, which recently unveiled a collaboration with the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris to preserve Schlumberger’s archives, continues to honor the artistry of his paillonné pieces with its Enamel by Tiffany collection. The house, which employs some of the only remaining artisans skilled in the technique, is expanding these offerings this fall with new pieces that include rings and watches. Despite the decades that have passed since the Croisillon’s debut, Cordier still finds it to be fresh. “When you look at the Schlumberger pieces, there’s this sort of abstract effect,” he says. “I think it’s very modern.”.

Cournot Raises $5M to Build AI-Native Oracle for Verifiable Intelligence

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cournot, a startup building an AI-native oracle that helps applications and AI agents understand and verify real-world events, has raised $5 million in a strategic funding round co-led by Paper Ventures and Beam Foundation, the company tweeted on Thursday.
  • Sources indicate that the firm was previously backed by YZi Labs, the investment firm of Binance founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao, through its EASY Residency Season 3 program.
  • Cournot has raised $5M co-led by @papervc and @BeamFDN following earlier backing from @yzilabs through @EASYResidency S3, to build the verifiable intelligence layer for onchain applications and AI agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cournot, a startup building an AI-native oracle that helps applications and AI agents understand and verify real-world events, has raised $5 million in a strategic funding round co-led by Paper Ventures and Beam Foundation, the company tweeted on Thursday.

Sources indicate that the firm was previously backed by YZi Labs, the investment firm of Binance founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao, through its EASY Residency Season 3 program. Cournot mentioned it will use the funding to develop its products, expand integrations on BNB Chain and other ecosystems, and move into areas including real-world assets, trading, parametric insurance, private credit and AI agents.

Cournot has raised $5M co-led by @papervc and @BeamFDN following earlier backing from @yzilabs through @EASYResidency S3, to build the verifiable intelligence layer for onchain applications and AI agents.

Cournot's mission is to expand what oracles can do: from structured data… pic.twitter.com/u0GnIBYFOO.

— Cournot Protocol (@CournotProtocol) November 26, 2026.

In a recent development, "As more financial activity and autonomous systems move onchain, the infrastructure around them needs to evolve beyond simply delivering data," Danish Chaudhry, founder of co-lead investor Paper Ventures, mentioned in a statement. Cournot is making real-world intelligence "more verifiable, auditable, and usable by both applications and AI agents," he added.

Sources indicate that oracles bring outside information onto blockchains, so smart contracts can act on it. Most deliver structured data, such as asset prices. Cournot is aimed at questions that need interpretation, such as whether a real-world event has happened or whether the available evidence meets a contract's rules.

Its Resolution Oracle uses AI to judge whether defined conditions have been met, while its Intelligence Oracle provides probabilities, claims and supporting sources before an outcome is known.

Both products rely on a framework Cournot calls Proof of Reasoning, which is designed to show how an AI model reached a conclusion, rather than just the conclusion itself.

Sources indicate that in a case study published in February, Cournot outlined a four-stage process. First, the system fixes what a question's terms mean before any evidence is gathered, and commits that definition as a cryptographic hash, so it cannot be reinterpreted later. It then collects evidence only from sources named in advance, within set time windows.

— Cournot Protocol (@CournotProtocol) February 7, 2026.

Where a source may change, such as a government webpage, Cournot uses  zkTLS, a cryptographic technique that proves a website displayed certain information at a given time, to keep a tamper-proof record. Finally, the AI's reasoning can only draw on that verified evidence, and its verdict follows from the predefined rules, leaving a trail that can be audited and challenged.

Industry observers note that the case study used a Polymarket market on whether there would be another U.S. government shutdown. Cournot has also cited a November 2025 shutdown market in which traders who correctly predicted the end date lost, because the Office of Personnel Management's website was updated a day after President Donald Trump signed the funding bill.

Cournot is also targeting the growing agent economy, in which autonomous AI agents need reliable outside information before making financial or operational decisions. Through its Intelligence Oracle skill, agents can request structured probabilities for events, the exact claims being assessed and supporting sources, and build those evidence-backed assessments into their own decision-making, according to the company.

Sources indicate that as of November 25, 2026, Cournot’s Resolution Oracle had settled more than $1.41 billion in notional value across more than 29,200 resolutions, with 99.8% finalized without a dispute, the firm remarked. The firm said resolutions had grown fivefold over the past three months and that the business is already profitable. Its oracles are used by prediction markets, agentic trading venues and trading card game platforms.

Its Intelligence Oracle Skill has scaled to more than 20,000 installs, 18,000 paying wallets and 967,000 paid calls, and the business is already profitable, according to Cournot. Its oracles are used by prediction markets, agentic trading venues and trading card game platforms.

Cournot argues the same problem applies well beyond betting, envisaging AI systems that could settle crop insurance by analyzing satellite imagery and local reports, or pay out on software contracts by reading a project's GitHub activity, with an auditable record of how each decision was reached.

"Human voting is slow and contestable, and black-box AI is fast but unaccountable," Cournot co-founder Daniel Wang noted in a statement.

Cournot remarked that at no stage is an outcome decided by a token-weighted vote. That is how disputes are settled on prediction market Polymarket, which relies on UMA's Optimistic Oracle, a system that has drawn criticism after disputed outcomes. Polymarket has also integrated Chainlink data feeds for markets that hinge on asset prices.

Cournot pointed to a November 2025 post in which CZ mentioned the industry needed more oracles, adding that "one or two is not enough.".

In the longer term, the firm stated its aim is to extend oracles beyond structured data into interpreting real-world events, providing verifiable intelligence and, eventually, taking action on behalf of AI agents within set policies. As more applications and autonomous agents operate onchain, the company expects demand to grow for infrastructure that helps them understand real-world information and weigh the evidence before they act.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amflow has made a name for itself in the electric mountain bike world with its high-performance Avinox-powered machines, but now the company is bringing that same technology to a decidedly more urban environment.
  • And while these might look like fairly conventional step-through city bikes at first glance, there’s some seriously impressive technology hiding beneath those clean lines.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amflow has made a name for itself in the electric mountain bike world with its high-performance Avinox-powered machines, but now the company is bringing that same technology to a decidedly more urban environment. The newly unveiled Amflow UE Carbon series marks the brand’s first move into the commuter e-bike market, combining a lightweight carbon fiber frame, powerful mid-drive motor, and a surprisingly long list of smart features designed for everyday riding.

And while these might look like fairly conventional step-through city bikes at first glance, there’s some seriously impressive technology hiding beneath those clean lines.

The new Amflow UE series comes in two versions, the UE Carbon and the higher-end UE Carbon Pro, both built around a full-carbon fiber frame weighing just 2.35 kg (5.2 lb).

The complete bike weighs as little as 20.9 kg (46 lb), which is fairly impressive considering the amount of hardware Amflow has packed into it, including front suspension, a suspension dropper seatpost, integrated lighting, and cargo racks.

Both models use the Avinox M2 mid-drive motor, which delivers up to 125 Nm of torque. That’s an enormous amount of torque for a city bike, and should make short work of steep hills, especially when carrying groceries or other cargo. And to put things into perspective, a lot of city e-bikes have barely 60 Nm for torque, so Amflow is knocking it out of the park for urban power.

A removable 600 Wh battery provides a claimed maximum range of 132 km (82 miles) in the lowest power assist mode, while fast charging can refill the battery in just 2 hours and 23 minutes.

The bikes also feature Avinox’s intelligent traction control system and a fresh Auto Boost function that automatically provides additional assistance when the system detects demanding conditions, such as accelerating from a stop or climbing a steep hill.

In other words, riders get much of the sophisticated motor technology developed for high-performance electric mountain bikes, but in a package designed for commuting to work or picking up groceries.

The bike is listed as weighing 20.9 kg (46 lb), though that figure conveniently excludes the front and rear racks, mudguards, pedals, kickstand, bike lock, bottle cage, and chainguard. So figure a few extra pounds for all of that gear, and you’re in the right ballpark.

The main difference between the two models is their drivetrain.

The higher-end UE Carbon Pro ($3,899) uses a customized three-speed electronically shifted internally geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt drive. That should make it particularly appealing to commuters who want a quiet, clean, low-maintenance setup without worrying about chain lubrication or derailleur adjustments.

The more affordable UE Carbon ($3,499) instead uses a 10-speed electronic derailleur developed with TRP.

Both models support automatic shifting, allowing the bike to handle gear changes without requiring the rider to constantly think about them.

Amflow has also gone fairly wild with the technology integration.

There’s a 1.4-inch touchscreen display mounted on the handlebars, a wireless phone charging mount offering 15W wireless charging or 20W USB-C charging, and integrated lighting with automatic low-light activation and brake-sensing functionality.

The bikes even include a hardened steel frame lock on the rear wheel, Apple Find My integration, and a Lost Mode feature that can lock down certain components if the bike is stolen.

Apple Watch connectivity allows riders to check their bike’s status and unlock it, while heart-rate-based assistance can automatically adjust motor output to help riders maintain a target heart rate zone.

Some of these features, like the security and tracking, are immediately effective for nearly all riders, while other high-tech features like the heart rate-based pedal assist can provide even more functionality for niche riders looking to bridge the gap between riding for transportation and riding for fitness.

Of course, all the fancy technology in the world doesn’t mean much if a commuter bike can’t handle everyday errands.

Fortunately, Amflow appears to have taken the practical side seriously.

The bikes feature a low step-through frame, upright riding position, 65 mm suspension fork, and a suspension dropper seatpost offering 125 mm of height adjustment and approximately 30 mm of suspension travel.

The 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires should also provide a comfortable ride over less-than-perfect city streets.

There’s a front rack rated for 20 kg (44 lb) and a rear rack rated for 27 kg (59.5 lb), with the latter supporting the MIK HD mounting system for compatible accessories, including child seats.

The standard frame is designed to accommodate riders from 155 to 190 cm (5’1” to 6’3”), while a smaller version for riders down to 140 cm (4’7”) is expected in 2027.

I’ve been impressed with the technology coming out of the Avinox ecosystem, and it’s exciting to see that technology finally make its way into a more practical city-focused electric bicycle.

It has been revealed that as much as I love high-performance electric mountain bikes, the reality is that most people aren’t spending their mornings bombing down mountain trails. They’re commuting to work, dropping kids off at school, and running errands.

And that’s where electric bicycles can make an even bigger difference.

Industry observers note that the Amflow UE series seems to take a refreshingly comprehensive approach to urban riding. The powerful motor is nice, but I’m arguably more interested in the belt drive, integrated security, cargo capacity, automatic shifting, and built-in phone charging.

Industry observers note that those are the kinds of features that can make an electric bicycle genuinely easier to live with every day. And as someone who actually commutes with an e-bike each day as my main form of transportation, these bikes are really speaking to me!

If you ask me, it’s great to see another high-performance e-bike manufacturer recognizing that the future of electric bicycles isn’t just about riding farther and faster on trails. It’s also about making everyday transportation better for the less exciting type of riding, too.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)

To Heal Your Heart, Purge Your Playlist

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • In a recent development, since I was old enough to record playlists on cassette tapes, I’ve paired music with my intense crushes.
  • According to recent reports, I fell in love with my college boyfriend to the tune of Bruce Springsteen’s “Dancing in the Dark,” while Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue was the anthem that played throughout a 15-year situationship with an elusive artist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, since I was old enough to record playlists on cassette tapes, I’ve paired music with my intense crushes. Each guy basically had his own song, sometimes an entire soundtrack.

According to recent reports, I fell in love with my college boyfriend to the tune of Bruce Springsteen’s “Dancing in the Dark,” while Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue was the anthem that played throughout a 15-year situationship with an elusive artist. Then, there was the whirlwind romance with a former smoke jumper turned ER doctor whose last concert was Emmylou Harris, which reminded me of the then-popular song “Emmylou” by First Aid Kit.

Recent findings suggest that each time, I became as obsessed with the song as the guy associated with it. My brain hyperfixated on the lyrics, first looking for hopeful clues, and then after the romance ended, sparking memories of sweet moments.

Sources indicate that music is often seen as a source of comfort for those dealing with heartbreak, but it can actually “arouse feelings of romantic longing, particularly searing melody,” indicates Walter Frisch, PhD, a professor of music at Columbia University. Some composers call such a haunting melody “l’idée fixe” or “fixed idea.”.

Industry observers note that once that “fixed idea” gets stuck in your head—in the form of a song played on repeat—it can actually trigger the thoughts that land you in limerence, the involuntarily obsessive rumination on an idealized love interest. It’s fueled by both the hope that the person you like likes you back and the uncertainty of whether they do.

For a long time, I thought I was alone in my lyric-fueled limerence, but as I interviewed experts and other limerents as research for my memoir, When Longing Becomes Your Lover, I learned that it’s incredibly common—and normal—for our brains to connect music with unrequited lovers.

Neuroscience would call this melody intermittent reinforcement. When we are infatuated with someone, we are anticipating connection with that person, which results in our brain’s reward system releasing the “feel good” hormone dopamine. As a result, we are motivated to return to the behavior of deeply thinking, or ruminating, about them to get that reward.

In one famous MRI brain scan study, when heartbroken individuals were shown pictures of their heartbreakers, their dopamine pathways lit up just as they would from doing cocaine. Similarly, music can trigger someone to ruminate about what could be or what could have been with a romantic interest, notes psychiatrist Jud Brewer, MD, PhD, the director of research and innovation at Brown University’s Mindfulness Center and author of The Craving Mind. The result, he says, is an itchy, contracted, restless feeling—quite the opposite of the expansive feeling associated with the mindfulness used to stop craving and anxiety.

Nostalgia also triggers the release of dopamine, and a song is like a time machine. Anytime I hear “Dancing in the Dark,” I’m instantly transported to kissing my college boyfriend in a dark, musty stairwell off campus. I can feel his hands resting on my hips and taste the Kentucky bourbon on his lips.

“There’s this certain charge you can get remembering somebody that you've been with before,” says Geoff MacDonald, PhD, a social psychologist who studies singlehood and sexuality at the University of Toronto. “You can replay, sort of viscerally, what it felt like to have somebody who was into you [and] that has the potential to provide real validation.”.

He points to one study on song lyrics and attachment styles that, he claims, “provides some evidence that people are drawn to a self-reinforcing bubble when it comes to intimacy.” In other words, it’s a form of confirmation bias. You’re drawn to songs with lyrics that reinforce what you already think about relationships, and you’re more likely to read into those lyrics and apply them to your own life.

According to recent reports, for example, if you have an anxious attachment style—which many limerents do—you typically feel insecure in relationships and fear abandonment. Consequently, you may need constant validation, which is exactly what a certain song can provide. When I heard “Emmylou” playing on the radio one morning after the sexy smoke jumper had grown more distant over text, I decided it was a sign from the universe that we were still meant to be together. (It wasn’t.).

Recent findings suggest that so, what’s a forlorn lover to do? Purge your playlist. “When someone is addicted to a behavior, if they avoid the people, places, and things [associated with the behavior], they’re less likely to get triggered to do the behavior,” indicates Brewer. “It’s not a great long-term solution, but it's one step that they can take.”.

According to recent reports, think of songs that trigger you to ruminate, whether you’re obsessing over a crush or languishing over a lost love. Maybe it’s a song whose lyrics remind you of them, or a tune you danced to together. Whatever it is, consider removing that song from your playlist—at least until hearing the first few notes no longer launches you into a two-hour daydream about your love interest.

Now, if you've got a playlist that you play once every couple of weeks when you're feeling lonely, that can probably stay in your Spotify rotation. “It's good to remember that you can be loved,” MacDonald indicates. “But if you're leaning into that as a replacement for actually seeking real intimacy in your life, that's where you're going to run into problems.”.

In a recent development, instead of relying on songs to dream about relationships that would never materialize, I deliberately poured that relentless energy into hobbies that gave my life purpose. That might look like spending quality time with a loved one, creating art, or planning a trip—anything that takes your mind off the individual and fills your self-worth bucket.

Now, I can listen to Kind of Blue and “Emmylou” without yearning for past lovers, but I prefer playing songs that reinforce the security I feel in my marriage, like “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” the song we walked down the aisle to.

Amanda McCracken is a journalist, writing professor at the University of Colorado, the author of When Longing Becomes Your Lover, and the host of The Longing Lab podcast.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ford has entered the battery business. The first LFP battery cells are now rolling off the assembly line at Ford’s BlueOval Battery Park plant in Michigan and are headed to power Fathom prototypes in Kentucky.

Recent findings suggest that how do you get more out of a battery without adding weight or more cells? According to Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, who is also leading its Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, the answer lies in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology.

Sources indicate that unlike traditional lithium-ion, LFP batteries use no nickel or cobalt, which helps reduce costs. They also typically hold up better after years of use and charging.

Sources indicate that to make it a reality, Ford turned to CATL, the leading global EV battery manufacturer. Ford uses CATL’s licensed technology and manufacturing expertise at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan plant.

Ford remarked it will be the first in the US to deliver LFP batteries for mainstream automotive use, with the battery cells now rolling off the line in Michigan.

The first LFP battery cells are headed to Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant and will be used to power Fathom prototypes, its first vehicle based on the UEV platform.

Ford designed and engineered the Fathom from the ground up for efficiency. As such, it chose prismatic battery cells because they fit directly into the chassis, reducing structural costs.

With cells now being delivered from a plant that it owns and operates, Ford remarked it will use the knowledge gained in Michigan to support more affordable EVs and Ford Energy, its fresh battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

At Ford’s upcoming battery plant in Michigan, assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it one of the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside China.

Although the accelerated output drives down costs, Ford said employees use AI-powered image recognition and inspection tools to spot defects in real time and maintain quality.

“Our goal is to make defective cells so rare that we track their frequency per billion cells rather than per million,” Ford said.

With production testing now underway, Ford aims to have the battery pack plant in Michigan up and running in 2027, ahead of schedule.

Ford will open preorders for the Fathom in early 2027, starting at $28,350 for the standard-range model.

CEO Jim Farley said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last month that the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle based on the UEV platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Farley mentioned the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and still affordable. The starting MSRP is under $30,000, and the low cost of ownership is perfect for today’s market, he added.

Recent findings suggest that ford and Slate both producing vehicles with US-produced LFP batteries is a great milestone. Hopefully we can keep pushing our domestic battery supply chain forward.

Ford mentioned the Fathom will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and it will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

According to recent reports, the pickup will be the first vehicle to integrate Apple Maps directly into the navigation system. All versions will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving, with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, plus bidirectional charging capabilities.

Although we have yet to see it, Ford remarked the Fathom features a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

Ford has not revealed battery specs or range, but we do know the pickup will have an NACS port after several prototypes were spotted at a Tesla Supercharger over the summer.

  • There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.
  • The one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee.
  • Sources indicate that despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.

The one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee. I am so hopelessly addicted to the stuff that I usually need at least one cup of coffee before going out to meet a friend for coffee.

Sources indicate that despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health. Throughout my lifetime, coffee has variously been purported to protect my heart, disrupt its rhythm, reduce my risk of cancer, and increase it. All I know is it helps me become a fully conscious person every morning. But could my coffee habit actually reduce wrinkles and help me age more gracefully?

A new study conducted at Texas A&M suggests that certain compounds in coffee might protect the body against aging and inflammation.

According to recent reports, however, according to Dr. Dung Trinh, the chief medical officer at Healthy Brain Clinic in Long Beach, California, it’s probably too soon to pop open the champagne (or brew a celebratory pot) over the potential perks of your coffee habit.

“It’s far too early to treat coffee—or caffeic acid—as an anti-aging intervention,” Trinh tells Popular Science.

Despite its inconsistent status as a health food, coffee has been consistently linked to longer life and a lower likelihood of certain diseases, though it’s not certain why. The Texas A&M study, led by Dr. Stephen Safe, focused on a cellular receptor called NR4A1.

NR4A1 is a protein that regulates how cells respond to stress and damage. The study found that several compounds in coffee, particularly polyphenols—plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties—bind to the NR4A1 receptor. One of these polyphenols, caffeic acid, is found in coffee and many other plants and, despite its name, has nothing to do with caffeine. These compounds seem to promote NR4A1’s protective effects, including mitigating cellular damage and slowing the growth of cancer cell line in laboratory models.

In other words, the harder your NR4A1 proteins are working, the better your cells may be at fending off damage. Sign me up!

Sources indicate that after researchers removed NR4A1 from cells in the lab, those benefits stopped, suggesting this receptor may help produce them. So, if coffee really helps NR4A1 do its job, we might just have a new anti-aging drink on our hands.

Interestingly, caffeine does not appear to play a key part in this mechanism, Trinh states. Instead, those benefits seem to come from coffee’s other compounds, like caffeic acid and its fellow polyphenols.

“What stood out to me was that the story was not really about caffeine,” he states. “I also found it interesting that the researchers did more than simply show that these compounds could bind to the receptor—they demonstrated NR4A1-dependent effects in cells. That makes the mechanism more compelling.”.

Translation: The study didn’t just show that coffee compounds attach to NR4A1; it showed that this binding actually seems to activate the protein’s protective effects.

Consistent with this, the study also found that decaf coffee demonstrated similar protective effects on the lab cells, providing further evidence that coffee’s benefits may not have anything to do with caffeine at all.

“One of the interesting messages from this paper is that coffee should not be thought of as simply a delivery system for caffeine,” Trinh says. “Caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, ferulic acid, and several other coffee compounds all interacted with NR4A1, while caffeine showed much more variable NR4A1-related activity.”.

So, coffee’s superpower might not come from caffeine at all, at least when it comes to anti-aging benefits.

Before you start guzzling triple lattes in the name of cellular protection, know that “more” does not always mean “better.”.

“We simply cannot infer from this study that more coffee means more NR4A1 benefit,” Trinh indicates. This is because the researchers studied coffee extracts and purified compounds in a lab setting rather than giving human subjects increasing amounts of coffee and measuring NR4A1 activity. Plus, in human biology, it’s possible to have too much of a good thing, Trinh says.

“At some point, additional coffee can bring unwanted effects from caffeine, including sleep disruption, anxiety, palpitations, or increases in blood pressure in susceptible people,” he notes. “Those effects could counteract other health benefits. So, this study should not be interpreted as establishing either an optimal number of cups or a dose-response relationship for this pathway.”.

Trinh adds that as compelling as the study’s findings are, he doesn’t yet believe they justify changing recommendations around coffee consumption.

Earlier studies have linked coffee drinking to living longer and to better outcomes for some age-related conditions, Trinh notes. But those studies couldn’t explain why. This one offers “one possible biological explanation,” he says.

Sources indicate that like most early-stage research, Trinh says, this study can’t be applied to humans sipping their morning “cup of ambition.” Much of the work used a specific cancer cell in the lab, along with mouse immune cells, rather than testing regular human coffee drinkers directly. And while the study identified a potentially promising mechanism, it’s not clear how this mechanism will translate to human health outcomes.

Ultimately, Trinh says, no single food or compound is likely to be the deciding factor in how well we age.

Sources indicate that for a coffee addict like myself, though, these findings are the best kind of wake-up call. Coffee may or may not turn back the clock, but it does stop me from hitting snooze 15 times.

“The much bigger determinants of healthy aging remain things such as regular physical activity, good sleep, avoiding smoking, controlling blood pressure and metabolic risk, maintaining social and cognitive engagement, and eating an overall nutritious diet,” Trinh notes.

“This study is a promising piece of the scientific puzzle, not a prescription for another cup of coffee.”.

A Minimalist House in Italy Makes the Case for Less

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in New York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein.
  • Pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint.
  • Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in New York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein. Pawson, then an architectural wunderkind from the United Kingdom, and Smith-Petersen, a young Danish-Italian communications manager for the fashion house, found themselves collaborating on the opening of the brand’s first flagship on Madison Avenue.

Pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint. His earliest residential works (a Mallorca summer house for collectors, an art dealer’s London apartment) provided a series of simple surfaces, plinths, and frames—for objects, for vistas, and for life. The same was true at the Calvin Klein store, where designer and client amplified each other’s design approaches in a meeting of minimalist minds.

Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.

The living area features a table and chairs by Poul Kjærholm.

A sauna is clad in blackened wood.

It has been revealed that pawson’s recent residence for Smith-Petersen and her husband, Enrico Erba Springorum, an Armani executive, makes another case for life with less. “The imprint came from childhood: the minimalism, the Danish design,” explains Smith-Petersen, who grew up outside Copenhagen. “Poul Kjærholm was our neighbor,” she adds, name-checking the widely influential midcentury modernist. There were also formative summers spent at the pared-back house her father designed on the Turkish peninsula of Çeşme. About the location, she recalls, “People remarked, ‘You guys are crazy!’ But it was a place close to nature and the sea. And then later it became a destination.”.

A single sculptural tree dots the courtyard.

An oak bed with integrated bedside tables anchors the primary bedroom.

Ninety minutes south of Milan, the patchwork hills of the Val Luretta are far less isolated. Its proximity to the city has attracted editors, artists, and other creatives in search of space and quiet. That tranquility drew Smith-Petersen to the area when she was seeking land on which to build a compound with her younger brother, Henrik, for their families. (She and her husband have two adult sons.) Over the years, she and Pawson had maintained a friendship. “So when Henrik and I found the property, I had this crazy idea: Why don’t I ask John?” says Smith-Petersen. “My brother stated, ‘Forget it!’ But we went to visit John and his team in London and it kicked off from there.”.

The primary bath’s bespoke vanity, topped in a Grassi Pietri surface.

Smith-Petersen stands in the living area.

A view across the dining table toward the minimalist hearth.

The resulting structure, realized with project architect Giulio Marchesi, is the irst of two planned homes on the site, one for each sibling. Sitting long and low on the land, like an ivory piano key dropped onto the hillside, the single-story house frames expansive views of the Val Luretta. “The area of the countryside is so dramatic,” reflects Pawson, whose first visit to the site was in winter fog. “In the summer, it’s very different—it’s so lush.”.

Sources indicate that at some 2,500 square feet, the house is spacious but intimate, with Pawson’s trademark spareness and remarkable warmth. He designed it along one axis, a long corridor connecting the foyer to the open-blueprint kitchen, dining area, and living area, then bedrooms beyond. White-painted plaster walls and floors of pale-gray stone, sourced nearby in Vicenza, radiate calm. As Pawson explains, understanding the way the body and the eye move through a space is paramount—and can take time. “You’ve got to learn the choreography,” he says. Living in and feeling the house is key.

Smith-Petersen and Pawson on-site.

Recent findings suggest that the yearslong friendship Pawson and Smith-Petersen had forged helped him understand how she would use the space. There would be mornings at the Pawson-designed table, afternoons on the terrace or under one of the century-old oaks, and evenings making dinner in a kitchen brimming with Scandinavian tableware. In solitude or surrounded by family, there’s complete peace on offer.

The open-initiative dining area and kitchen.

“Most architects—contemporaries, colleagues—always say, ‘Oh, it’s impossible, a private house,’ ” indicates Pawson. The process can be “very emotional. And that’s what makes it good.” Luckily for Smith-Petersen, the primary feeling the house evokes is serenity. “I didn’t expect to be in such awe,” she says. “I was never a country person. Sometimes, I try to arrive a day before anyone else is here and do a silent retreat,” she adds. “It’s where I feel best now. It’s pure joy.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, even Alaska’s bears are not immune from accidentally making things weird or getting a bit too close. Over the summer, rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska watched an odd interaction between two unnamed black bears (Ursus americanus) taking part in Anan Creek’s salmon run.

Industry observers note that “Sometimes the bears at Anan share the creek… a little too closely,” the rangers write. “One bear is waiting his turn for a prime fishing spot, and the other is so focused on the fish he doesn’t mind his surroundings. Did the 1st bear make it weird by backing up, or did the 2nd bear make it weird by staying there?”.

For this bit of humor, the rangers awarded the unnamed bears with the 2026 You Made it Weird Award.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

The largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in the region. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Latest Update: West Coast Customs turns a Tesla Model 3 into a 1955 Chevy Bel Air

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • West Coast Customs has finished its first electric Chevy Bel Air, and there’s not much Chevy left under the paint.
  • In a recent development, the result, called Project B-Zero, looks like a ’55 Chevy from the curb and like a Model 3 as soon as you open the door.
  • In the shop’s latest video, “The First Ever Electric Bel Air,” founder and CEO Ryan Friedlinghaus explains that a longtime client, Troy Swope, wants to convert an entire car collection to electric and picked the Bel Air to go first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Coast Customs has finished its first electric Chevy Bel Air, and there’s not much Chevy left under the paint. The Burbank shop cut the body off a Tesla Model 3, kept the entire rolling platform, and set a 1955 Bel Air shell on top of it.

In a recent development, the result, called Project B-Zero, looks like a ’55 Chevy from the curb and like a Model 3 as soon as you open the door. And it charges at Tesla Superchargers.

In the shop’s latest video, “The First Ever Electric Bel Air,” founder and CEO Ryan Friedlinghaus explains that a longtime client, Troy Swope, wants to convert an entire car collection to electric and picked the Bel Air to go first. WCC had previously built the same client a Chevelle with a major gas engine.

Recent findings suggest that friedlinghaus, who drives a Tesla himself, decided against pulling the Model 3’s motors and battery out and fitting them into the old Chevy. Instead, the Tesla stays whole and the Chevy becomes the body kit.

That’s a formula WCC has used for years with gas cars. The shop calls it “old school meets fresh school”: an old GTO body on a new GTO, an old Camaro on a new Camaro, an old Mustang on a new Mustang. B-Zero is the first time it did it with a Tesla underneath.

“It sounds easy, but that process was tedious,” Friedlinghaus mentioned.

Before any Chevy sheet metal went on, the crew took the bare Model 3 skateboard for a spin on the streets around the shop, with no doors, no lights and no seatbelts. Friedlinghaus joked about how many safety violations they were racking up. But it drove fine.

Recent findings suggest that the real headache was the wheelbase. A 1955 Chevy rides on a 115-inch wheelbase, while the Model 3 sits at 113.2 inches. On its gas builds, WCC can cut, shorten or lengthen the newer car’s frame to match the old body. You can’t do that with a Tesla, since the floor is the battery pack.

So the shop changed the body instead, stretching the Bel Air’s rear wheel wells so the wheels sit where they look like they belong.

The client wanted the exterior to read as a mostly stock Bel Air. The original car was red, so WCC kept it red, with a satin finish and gloss black accents.

Inside, it’s a Model 3. The shop kept the Tesla’s interior, including the steering wheel and center touchscreen, and modified it to fit the Chevy body. The seats got black suede with white stitching in an octagon pattern that Friedlinghaus mentioned was borrowed from the Lamborghini Urus, plus red accents and a “B-Zero” script on the dash.

It has been revealed that friedlinghaus said the goal was for people to see “a really nice Bel Air” from the outside, then open the door and find a Tesla. He also expects some double takes when it pulls into a Supercharger station.

He admits the reaction has been split. Plenty of people are mad that the shop electrified a Bel Air, and plenty of others think it came out great. The client is clearly in the second camp, describing the car as easy to drive and saying every trip in it feels like an event.

Here’s the full build video from West Coast Customs:.

Industry observers note that this is sick. I know Tesla doesn’t care about personal car ownership anymore, but they should really sell their platform so shops can do these conversions without using salvage vehicles.

Industry observers note that well I was really interested in this build until I read how they kept it entirely Tesla inside. Not at all what I was thinking or what I'd call a true old car conversion to EV. Instead, they simply transformed the outside of a Tesla into an old looking car. To me, even the outside looks too far removed from the original Bel Air and more like a street rod. If that's what the owner wants and paid for, great.

Industry observers note that but for me, I would never do a conversion like that. I really want to convert an older 70's or 80's or early 90's Cadillac into an EV. But for me, I will insist that the outside and inside look 100% like the original car with just an EV powertrain.

Don’t get me wrong, if you can recycle a salvage, that’s good, but it can’t always be done.

Sources indicate that compare it to the 1966 Mustang that a Sacramento Tesla parts shop converted earlier this year. That project took about $40,000 and two years, with the team grafting sections of a Model 3 floor into the Mustang. It’s an amazing build, but it’s a lot of custom engineering. WCC’s approach skips most of that. You keep Tesla’s crash structure, battery thermal management, software, over-the-air updates and Supercharger access, because you never took the car apart in the first place. It’s closer to what S-Klub did with its Model 3-based Mercedes 300SL than a traditional drivetrain swap.

Recent findings suggest that the purists will hate it. That’s fine. This Bel Air will get driven more in a year than most restored ones get driven in a decade.
